opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's actually more continuity there than it might look like from the outside. The thing I was really excited about in grad school, with the neural module networks work, was this question of how you get the compositional structure of language to show up in the structure of a learned model. The idea was: if you have a question like "what color is the thing to the left of the dog," language is already telling you something about how to decompose that problem into pieces, and you can use that to assemble a little custom network on the fly out of reusable parts. So language served as a kind of scaffold for computation.

What happened over the following years is that the field moved in a direction where you don't build that structure in by hand anymore. You train very big, very general models, and a lot of the compositional behavior we were trying to engineer just sort of emerges, or at least emerges well enough that the explicit modular machinery stopped being the most productive thing to work on. I think one lesson I took from that is to be a little humble about which inductive biases you actually need to bake in versus which ones you can get from data and scale.

But the underlying questions didn't go away. They just moved. Instead of asking "how do we build models with compositional structure," a lot of what my lab does now is ask "what structure do these models already have, and how can we find it, measure it, and use it?" So there's a big interpretability and analysis component: do language models build anything like representations of the world, or of the people they're talking to, or of the state of a program they're reading? And then there's the flip side, which is still very much about language as a tool for learning, using natural language explanations, instructions, or descriptions to help models generalize better, learn new abstractions, or learn from much less data. That's pretty directly descended from the module networks idea, that language isn't just an output, it's something that can shape how a system reasons.

And increasingly we care about the interaction side: models that can ask questions, figure out what people actually want, update their beliefs in a coherent way. So if I had to draw one thread through all of it, it's that I've always been interested in language less as a task to be solved and more as this incredibly rich source of structure about the world and about how to think. The methods have changed a lot, but that's been pretty constant.

r001.rationale: The response says explicit modular machinery became less productive as the field shifted, while the underlying questions continued as the lab’s work on finding, measuring, and using structure in models.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a scaffold for computation and says the lab still uses language to shape how systems reason.

r003.rationale: The response says language explanations, instructions, and descriptions can improve generalization and abstraction, but does not identify language as supervising representations for other tasks.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss establishing an independent lab as developing a research direction that can accommodate other researchers.

r005.rationale: It describes a shift toward interpretability and analysis, but does not say that this work is model-agnostic.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the ModuleNet stuff, or neural module networks as we ended up calling them, came out of this very specific observation. This was around 2015, and we were trying to do visual question answering. The dominant approach was to take a big convolutional net, take a big recurrent net, glue them together, and hope that whatever representation came out in the middle was enough to answer the question. And it worked okay, but it was clear that it was failing in ways that had to do with the structure of the questions themselves. You'd ask something like "what color is the thing to the left of the dog," and the model had no mechanism for actually finding the dog, then looking left, then reading off a color. It would just pattern-match on surface features.

The idea behind module networks was that language already comes with a compositional structure, and that structure tells you something about how to compose a computation. So you parse the question, and the parse tells you which small neural network pieces to assemble and in what order. A module for finding things, a module for spatial relations, a module for classifying attributes. The reasoning procedure is dynamically built from the sentence.

Looking back, I think the thing I was actually interested in there wasn't really vision, or even question answering. It was this question about the relationship between the structure of language and the structure of the computations that models perform. Language is this remarkably efficient, compressed way of specifying what you want done. And in ModuleNet, we were using it almost as a programming language, as a way of directly wiring up a model.

What's happened since then, obviously, is that the field moved toward much larger, much less structured models, and a lot of the explicit compositionality that we were building in by hand turned out to be something that these systems could pick up, at least partially, from data. For a while I think that felt like a refutation of the module network program. But I actually think the underlying questions just got more interesting rather than going away.

So one thread in the lab now is about interpretability, and it's really the same question turned around. Instead of asking how do we use language to build a model's computation, we're asking whether we can use language to describe the computation that a model learned on its own. Can we take a neuron, or a circuit, or a feature inside a big network and produce a natural language explanation of what it's doing, and then actually verify that the explanation is faithful? That's the lineage from module networks pretty directly, it's just that the direction of the arrow has flipped.

The other big thread is about language as a medium for learning, not just for specifying tasks. Humans don't learn most things from reward signals or from thousands of labeled examples. We learn an enormous amount from someone telling us things. "The bird with the red crest is a cardinal." "Don't touch that, it's hot." And so a lot of what we think about now is how to build agents that can take linguistic supervision, instructions, explanations, corrections, and turn it into changes in behavior or in their internal representations. That includes work on whether language models themselves form something like world models, and what it would mean for them to update those models when you tell them something.

And then there's a strand that's more about the models as objects of scientific study. Once you have systems that are good enough at language that you can run something like a psycholinguistics experiment on them, you can start asking questions about what they've actually acquired and how. That connects back to older interests in computational linguistics and cognitive science that were honestly always lurking under the ModuleNet work.

So if I had to compress it, I'd say the PhD was about the idea that the structure of language is a good prior for the structure of computation. And the lab now is about the broader set of relationships between language, learning, and the internal organization of intelligent systems, whether that's a neural network or a person. The specific technical tools have changed almost completely. The question, I think, is pretty much the same one.

r001.rationale: It says explicit compositionality in ModuleNet was partly learned by larger models, which seemed to refute that program, but the underlying questions remain and now inform the lab’s interpretability work.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a way to wire up computation in ModuleNet and says the lab still studies the relationship between language and computation, including using language to describe learned computations.

r003.rationale: It identifies linguistic supervision—such as instructions, explanations, and corrections—as a way to change agents’ behavior or internal representations.

r004.rationale: It does not present accommodating researchers beyond oneself as part of establishing an independent lab.

r005.rationale: It describes a move toward studying interpretability in learned networks, but does not characterize that work as model-agnostic.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a fairly consistent thread, which is an interest in how language connects to other kinds of computation. With the neural module networks work during my PhD, the question was: can we use the structure of a question to help determine the structure of the computation that answers it? If you’re answering a question about an image, for example, you might want to find something, identify a property of it, and compare it with something else. The idea was to build those operations out of learned components and use language to put them together.

That opens up a broader question: what role can language play in helping us build systems that learn and generalize? Language isn’t just something we want a model to produce. It’s also a way for people to communicate tasks, describe useful abstractions, and pass along knowledge without demonstrating every possible situation.

So I see the evolution less as leaving those early questions behind and more as broadening them. There’s the question of how language can guide learning and reasoning, and then there’s the question of what the models themselves have learned: what representations support their behavior, and how we can understand and steer them. The common interest is in the relationship between the flexibility of learned systems and the structure that language gives us.

r001.rationale: The response says the early questions broadened, but does not say ModuleNet itself had limited staying power or contrast that with the continuing influence of its interpretability questions.

r002.rationale: It describes language helping determine computational structure and assemble learned operations, then identifies language-guided learning and reasoning as part of the broadened research direction.

r003.rationale: The response says language can communicate tasks and useful abstractions, but does not identify using it to supervise representations for other tasks.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss establishing an independent lab or developing a research direction that accommodates other researchers.

r005.rationale: It mentions understanding and steering model representations, but does not describe a transition to model-agnostic interpretability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a fairly continuous thread, which is this question of how language can help us build systems that learn and generalize better. In the ModuleNet work, that took a very explicit form: could we take the structure of a question and use it to assemble a computation? If you asked a different question, we could reuse familiar pieces in a new combination, rather than having to learn the whole mapping from scratch.

That approach also raised a broader question: how much structure should we build into a model, and how much can it discover from data? You don’t necessarily want to prescribe every component or every way those components can interact. But you do want the system to be able to reuse what it knows in a new situation.

So I see the connection to the questions we pursue now as moving from language as a specification of a computation toward language as a more general resource for learning and communication. How can an explanation help a learner? How can a system figure out what someone means, or communicate something that helps them accomplish a task? The architectures have changed, but the underlying interest is still in how language lets us transfer knowledge and put familiar ideas together in new ways.

r001.rationale: The response describes continuity from ModuleNet but does not say the work itself had limited staying power or that its interpretability questions continued to influence the lab.
